web_evidence.title: Excerpt from Hannibal by Thomas Harris
web_evidence.note: Publisher-permission excerpt from Chapter 21 moves from rhetorical reader guidance into sustained external narration of Lecter's actions, history, perceptions, and thoughts; the narrator is not a story character.

web_evidence.title: Hannibal by Thomas Harris on Apple Books
web_evidence.note: The displayed Publishers Weekly review explicitly describes the novel's technique as third-person-plural narration, explaining its narratorial we as reader complicity rather than a participating character.

web_evidence.title: Enamoured or Enemies? Analysing focalisation and space in Harris' novel and its adaptation
web_evidence.note: This scholarly close reading finds shifting internal character focalisation and external focalisation by an anonymous agent. In conjunction with the prose evidence, that structure supports a nonparticipating third-person base narrator.

web_evidence.title: Hannibal Lecter Judges Me When I Cook
web_evidence.note: A writer's craft analysis identifies Harris's third-person omniscient technique and discusses specific Hannibal scenes in which narration moves outside and inside Lecter's perspective.

Ran targeted exact-line searches to resolve apparent contrary passages: q00274 is Starling's free-direct thought, q00276 is speech reported by Barney, q00307 is part of Lecter's letter, and q00287 is narrator-to-reader rhetoric. A full-text PDF on an unverified host was used only for contextual discovery and was excluded from web evidence.
person_note: The controlling narrator is a nonparticipating third-person voice that shifts focalisation among Starling, Lecter, Pazzi, Crawford, and others. The diagnostic event quotes agree with the authorized Chapter 21 excerpt and the structural web sources. Apparent first-person material is local: q00274 is Starling's thought, q00276 is reported speech, and q00307 is Lecter's letter. Chapter 21's you/we language guides the reader through the setting as a spectator; it does not cast a story protagonist as you or turn the narrator into a character. Thus the rhetorical pronoun play does not create alternating base narration. The remaining uncertainty concerns only these local stylistic intrusions, not the whole-book structure.
